query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Al content in CrFeCoNiX (with X = Al) high-entropy alloys will promote controlled Al diffusion that enables the formation and persistence of a coherent, slow-growing αAl2O3 scale at temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments, reducing the tendency for oxide cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with baseline (non-optimized) Al content where oxide scales are unstable.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by enhancing the Al concentration (and possibly tuning minor additions to mimic TiAl alloy modifications) to facilitate controlled surface diffusion of Al.
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere (e.g., air or a controlled oxygen environment).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent, slow-growing αAl2O3 oxide layer that acts as a continuous protective barrier.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced Al content increases the driving force for Al diffusion from the bulk to the surface. This promotes preferential nucleation and growth of a dense, adherent αAl2O3 scale, analogous to alloying strategies in TiAl systems. The coherent scale minimizes interfacial strain and prevents the buildup of stresses that could otherwise lead to cracking or spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline alloys, the modified high-Al-content alloy will develop a continuous, defect‐free αAl2O3 layer that remains stable without significant cracking or spallation during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNiX alloys with lower or non-optimized Al concentrations that typically form unstable oxide scales prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is tested on CrFeCoNiX HEAs (with X being Si, Mn, or optimized Al) under high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative or corrosive conditions, where the scale formation and integrity are critical.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise threshold of Al concentration required and the potential influence of other alloying elements (e.g., Si or Mn) on the kinetics of Al diffusion and oxide adherence. The interaction between multiple phases in the multiphase state may also affect scale formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy specimens: one with a baseline (lower) Al content and the other with an optimized higher Al content. Expose both sets to temperatures above 900 °C in a controlled oxidative atmosphere for an extended duration.
measurements: SEM imaging and EDS mapping of the oxide scale to assess continuity, composition, and presence of micro-cracks.
Measurement of the oxide scale growth kinetics and evaluation of spallation or cracking events during cyclic oxidation tests.
Quantitative weight gain measurements to compare oxidation rates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the higher Al content specimens do not exhibit a significantly more continuous and adherent αAl2O3 scale (with reduced cracking/spallation) compared to the baseline specimens, or if similar scale degradation is observed despite the intervention, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The intermetallic compounds of the Ti–Al system are known not to pest []. Aluminium rich TiAl, and the TiAl2 and TiAl3 aluminides can form alumina scales but Al poor TiAl and Ti3Al form titania rich scales and oxidise at much higher rates []. For example, when TiAl with 50 at.% Al was oxidised in air at 950, 1100 and 1200 °C, at the two higher temperatures TiO2 scale formed and there was internal oxidation. Parabolic oxidation kinetics were followed at the low temperature where the oxidation was independent of specimen preparation and fabrication method []. Furthermore, the alloying of TiAl with Nb promoted the formation of continuous alumina scale on TiAl (50 at.% Al) at 950 °C independent of surface preparation or exposure environment (air or O2) but the alloying with Hf had a minimal effect []. The alloying of TiAl with Si improved oxidation resistance []. For Al poor TiAl it is known that the addition of 4 to 12 at.% Nb in Ti–48Al increased oxidation resistance at 850 °C and that the alloys developed continuous bands of dense alumina beneath titania rich surface layer that formed during the early stages of oxidation []. The external scale was composed of an outer and an inner part with different oxides according to location. In the former, the AlNbO4, CrNbO4 and αAl2O3 oxides were observed, in the latter only the αAl2O3 was found (Figure 7). The NbAl3 formed the AlNbO4 (assumed to be a result of transient oxidation) above an inner Al2O3 layer in contact with the alloy (substrate). The Laves phase formed the CrNbO4 with an inner Al2O3 layer. In some areas of the alloy/scale interface the inner continuous Al2O3 layer was not formed, instead internal oxidation had occurred where alumina oxide was observed. Internal oxidation had occurred in all facets of the cubic specimen and was deeper along the phase boundaries (Figure 8). The internal oxidation is known to cause embrittlement of the substrate and to play a role in scale spallation. At 800 °C the integrity of the scale on OHC3 was practically intact. reading.lever: Adapt alloying strategies from TiAl systems to promote controlled Al diffusion for coherent protective αAl2O3 scale formation.
reading.why: Because TiAl-based modifications have successfully yielded continuous, slow-growing alumina scales, addressing similar instability issues observed in HEAs.
